prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. Starting in 1920, her reviews of every play, whether praised or faulted, ended with a sentence about what standing room cost the city's clerks and shopgirls. A later index of her columns finds that sentence in all but a handful of the reviews she wrote over the next eleven years. Theater managers' letters from 1931 name her column when the three largest theaters halved standing-room prices, and the closing sentences stopped the following week. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: She closed nearly every review for eleven years with the same point about standing-room prices, and stopped only once the theaters cut them, so she was "insistent." "Mercurial" fails because she held to one point in all but a handful of reviews; "jaded" fails because she kept the campaign going season after season rather than growing weary; "judicious" fails because the closing sentence appeared whatever the play, so the passage shows persistence, not careful weighing of plays.

mercurial.quote: in all but a handful of the reviews
mercurial.why: returning to one point in nearly every review for years is the reverse of changeable

jaded.why: keeping up a campaign for over a decade shows energy, not weariness

judicious.quote: every play, whether praised or faulted
judicious.why: the sentence ended her reviews regardless of her verdict on the play, so it shows persistence about prices, not discernment about plays

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. By her last decade she had reviewed well over two thousand productions. Her reviews from those years shrink to a single paragraph, and the word she used most often in them was "familiar." Several plays she dismissed that way were hailed as fresh by younger critics in the same season and ran for years. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: After thousands of productions, her reviews dwindled and she dismissed as familiar plays that others found fresh, so she had become "jaded." "Judicious" fails because the plays she waved off succeeded, so her verdicts did not reflect sound judgment; "mercurial" fails because her response was the same dismissal again and again; "insistent" fails because she was pressing no demand, only losing interest.

judicious.why: plays she waved off as familiar succeeded, so her verdicts reflect weariness, not good judgment

mercurial.quote: the word she used most often
mercurial.why: her reaction was the same over and over, which is consistency, not changeability

insistent.why: her reviews dwindled; she was withdrawing effort, not pressing a point

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. Theater managers and rival critics often mocked her reviews as timid, since they seldom joined the opening-night cheers or the walkouts. A later scholar compared every city critic's verdicts with what became of the plays over the following fifty years and found hers borne out most often: the plays she had praised were largely the ones still being staged, and those she had faulted had mostly been forgotten. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: Her reviews were restrained, and her verdicts proved right more often than any other critic's over fifty years, so she was "judicious." "Jaded" fails because she went on finding plays worth praising; "mercurial" fails because verdicts that held up across fifty years were not swinging with her moods; "insistent" fails because nothing shows her pressing any demand.

jaded.why: she praised plays throughout, so she had not grown weary of the stage

mercurial.quote: found hers borne out most often
mercurial.why: a critic whose verdicts consistently match the plays' later fates is steady, not changeable

insistent.why: her reviews were restrained, not forceful or repeated demands

worlds.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. In one season she called a play the finest of the year in March and, after seeing it again, tedious in April. The stage manager's logs show that the cast, the staging, and even the running time were unchanged between her two visits. Theater managers learned to quote her column in their advertisements only after a production had closed for the season. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
worlds.explanation: Her verdict on an unchanged play flipped within a month, and managers did not trust any verdict of hers to last, so she was "mercurial." "Jaded" fails because she was capable of calling a play the finest of the year; "judicious" fails because a verdict that flips while the play stays the same does not come from careful weighing; "insistent" fails because she held no position steadily.

jaded.why: a critic who can call a play the year's best has not grown weary of the stage

judicious.quote: were unchanged between her two visits
judicious.why: her verdict changed though the play did not, so the change came from her, not from the play

insistent.quote: only after a production had closed
insistent.why: managers waited because her opinion might change; she did not hold to a view
